Step 2: Reasoning

Your stew worked, so the basics are fine. The trouble likely comes from the recipes you moved on to. Plant-based dishes and yogurt behave differently from a meat stew. Vegetables and legumes cook at different rates, they release water, and yogurt depends on temperature control more than cooking time. Advice aimed at those areas will help most.

Step 3: Advice for better results

General slow cooker tips
- Use less liquid than you would on the stove. The lid traps moisture, so plant-based dishes can turn watery. Start with about two-thirds of the liquid a stovetop recipe calls for.
- Layer by cooking time. Put dense vegetables like potatoes, carrots, and sweet potatoes on the bottom near the heat. Add soft vegetables like zucchini and spinach in the last 30 to 60 minutes.
- Sauté onions, garlic, and spices first. Five minutes in a pan adds a lot of depth to lentil curries and bean chilis.
- Add dairy, coconut milk, fresh herbs, and acids (lemon, vinegar) near the end so they don't split or lose their brightness.
- Keep the lid on. Each peek can add 15 to 20 minutes of cooking time.
- Fill the cooker one-half to two-thirds full for even cooking.
- Watch dried beans. Kidney beans need a 10-minute hard boil before slow cooking to destroy a natural toxin. Acidic tomatoes can also keep beans from softening, so add them later or use canned beans.
- Skip dishes that rely on crisping. The breadcrumb-topped mac and cheese I suggested earlier won't crisp in a slow cooker. Toast the topping separately.

Cashew yogurt tips
A couple of points correct my earlier advice:
- Don't strain the cashew blend or throw out the solids. Well-soaked cashews blend completely smooth, and the solids are what make the yogurt thick. Straining will leave it thin.
- Don't heat cashew milk to 180°F like dairy milk. Just warm it to about 100 to 110°F, then stir in a vegan starter or probiotic.
- Keep the incubation temperature steady. Use the "warm" setting on and off, or turn the cooker off and wrap it in a towel. Too much heat kills the cultures.
- Cashew yogurt won't thicken like dairy yogurt. It firms up mostly after chilling. For extra thickness, add a little agar or tapioca starch.
- A thermometer helps more than any recipe tweak.

Step 2: Tips for getting around Tokyo, based on those plans:

Your Suica card
- Suica works on nearly all JR, Metro, Toei subway, and bus lines, plus convenience stores, vending machines, and many coin lockers. You can use it for almost all your daily travel.
- Top it up with cash at any station ticket machine. Most machines have an English button. Keep about ¥2,000 or more on the card so you're never stuck at a gate.
- If you're short at the exit gate, use the yellow "Fare Adjustment" machine next to the gates.

From Narita
- The Narita Express (N'EX) runs straight to Shinjuku in about 80 to 90 minutes. Every seat is reserved, so buy an N'EX ticket at the JR counter or ticket machine instead of only tapping your Suica. JR often sells a discounted round-trip N'EX ticket for foreign visitors.
- The Skyliner also needs its own ticket, and it means changing trains at Ueno. With luggage, N'EX is simpler.

Two corrections to my earlier advice
- Tsukiji route: Tsukijishijo Station is on the Toei Oedo Line, not the Ginza Line. The easiest route is to take the Oedo Line from Tochomae Station, which is the closest station to the Park Hyatt, or from Shinjuku Station straight to Tsukijishijo. It takes about 20 minutes with no transfers.
- Tsukiji market: the wholesale inner market and tuna auction moved to Toyosu Market in 2018. The Tsukiji Outer Market is still open and is the place for a sushi breakfast. If you want to see the auction, go to Toyosu, which is on the Yurikamome Line.

Tokyo Tower
- Take the Oedo Line from Tochomae or Shinjuku to Akabanebashi Station, about 5 minutes on foot from the tower.

Apps
- Google Maps handles Tokyo transit well. It shows platforms, which car to board, and exit numbers.
- Japan Transit Planner (Jorudan) or NAVITIME are useful backups.
- Get a pocket Wi-Fi or eSIM so you can check routes on the move.

Navigating stations
- Shinjuku Station is the busiest station in the world, so don't worry if it feels like a maze. Follow the color-coded line signs and exit numbers. Signs are in English.
- Use the numbered exits shown in your map app. Picking the right exit can save you 10 minutes of walking.
- Station staff are used to helping visitors. Showing them your destination on your phone works well.

Timing and etiquette
- Avoid trains from about 7:30 to 9:30 AM and from 5:30 to 7:30 PM on weekdays if you can, especially with luggage.
- Trains stop around midnight to 12:30 AM. After that you'll need a taxi.
- Stand on the left on escalators in Tokyo. Keep phone calls off trains, and wait in the marked lines on the platform.

Taxis
- Taxis are clean, safe, and honest, though not cheap. The rear door opens automatically, so don't grab it.
- The GO app works like Uber for Tokyo taxis. You can also have the hotel concierge write your destination in Japanese.

Step 3: Bottom line

With a topped-up Suica, Google Maps, and the Oedo Line from Tochomae near your hotel, you can reach most places on your list easily. Tokyo is one of the easiest and safest big cities to get around.
